sentences.text:
Accused JUDGMENT:
1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused Dev Raj is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Aggarwal Sweets Corner, from where the food article, that is, 'Besan ke laddu' was lifted for sampling.

2. As per the complaint, on 01.11.2010, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Virender Singh and Field Assistant (FA) S. N. Jindal under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Ajay Kumar reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Aggarwal Sweets Corner at B-6/114, Sector-8, Rohini, Delhi-110085, where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Besan ke laddu from the vendor, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama,
etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 24.11.2010, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained added vegetable oil which was not declared as an ingredient.

Upon receipt of Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj on 30 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65795867/
1 report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.

sentences.text: After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 09.02.2011 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (c) and (m) of PFA Act as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 09.02.2011.

The accused appeared but chose not to file any application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).

4. On the basis of PA report, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against the accused on 20.07.2011 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act,
being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (c) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. At the trial, prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.
PW-1 Sh. Ajay Kumar (SDM/LHA), PW-2 FI Virender Singh and PW-3 FA S. N. Jindal were examined who all were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

All these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 01.11.2010 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Besan ke laddu from an open tray, breaking the same into smallest possible pieces using a clean and dry spoon, mixing/homogenizing it using the same spoon, dividing it in three parts and putting in clean and dry bottles, adding formalin (40 drops each) as preservative, fastening, sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.
PW-1/A, Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B (on which the vendor disclosed the ingredients of the commodity) and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C. Raid report Ex. PW-1/D was also prepared at the spot and statement of accused Ex. PW-1/E
was recorded.
On the next day, one counterpart of the sample with Memo as per Form-VII was deposited with PA vide PA Receipt Ex.
PW-2/A and the other two counterparts with memos were deposited with LHA vide receipt Ex. PW-1/F. PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received upon which investigation was carried out by PW-2.
He sent letter Ex. PW-2/B to VAT Office to ascertain the constitution of the business concern.

After completion of investigation,
sanction Ex. PW-1/H was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/I was filed in the court.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/J was sent to the accused through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/K.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the some vanaspati was lying in the tray in which laddus had been broken.
They could not tell if there was any standard of 'extracted fat' in PFA Act or not.
6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 26.03.2014 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though he admitted the proceedings dated 01.11.2010, yet he claimed that no public person was requested to join the proceedings.
He denied receiving the PA report.
He questioned the PA report by claiming that some vegetable oil is put on the tray by the workers/karigars when they prepare the laddus so that they do not stick to the tray.
He however chose not to lead evidence in defence.

sentences.text: It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 24.11.2010.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample on question is a proprietary food for which there are no standards prescribed under the PFA Act or Rules.
It is submitted that no standards are there for 'extracted fat' which was analysed by the PA.
It is then argued that as per Rule 43(5) of PFA Rules, a seller of sweets is not required to declare the ingredients and thus, there is no violation of rules.

It is maintained that vegetable oil is allowed to be used on the tray of such food articles, as "good manufacturing practice" so that they may not stick to it, and such vegetable oil might have been detected by the PA.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused and have carefully perused the material available on record.
10. It is to be understood that the notice framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b), (c) and (m) of the PFA Act.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof.

Section 2(ia)(c) of PFA Act requires to be established that any inferior or cheaper substance has been substituted, wholly or in part, for the article so as to affect injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof.

On the other hand, section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
11. To begin with, it is an admitted position that the food article Besan ke laddu does not fall under any item of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules.
No standards have been prescribed under the Rules with respect to 'Besan ke laddu' as a standardised food article.
It was thus analysed as a proprietary food.
Proprietary Food, as per Rule 37-A of PFA Rules means a food which has not been standardised under the said Rules.
Under Rule 37-A(e), proprietary food products shall not contain food additives except as provided under the rules for that food or category of food.

12. It is then seen that the accused has not questioned the fact that the business concern M/s.
Aggarwal Sweets Corner was a proprietorship concern, of which he was the proprietor.
It is not his case that he was not the proprietor of the said premises or that some other person was its proprietor.

He rather admitted this fact in his statement under section 313 CrPC.
13.
It is again not disputed that a sample of Besan ke laddu was lifted by the food officials on 01.11.2010 from the said premises and the accused was the vendor who had sold the said article.

It is Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj on 30 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65795867/
3 not his stand that the food article was not for sale or that it was for any purpose other than sale for human consumption.

sentences.text: No defect or irregularity in the sample proceedings has been raised by the defence.
There is no dispute about the sample having been sent to the PA on the specified date in question.
There is no dispute that the complaint was filed as per the procedure after obtaining sanction / consent of the Director, PFA.
14. It is then seen that the accused has not exercised his right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.
For this, the arguments are that PA report with intimation letter were never served upon him.

15. As per the scheme of the Act, under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused,
informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA, after filing of the complaint.

It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and would be fatal to the prosecution because this right cannot be allowed to be frustrated by the prosecution.

However, if the accused himself forgoes his right,
then he cannot say that he was prejudiced.
16. At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused.
PW-1 and PW-2 both deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/J through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/K.
The original intimation letter and postal receipts had been produced during the evidence of PW-1 which were then exhibited.
No objection had been raised by the Ld. Defence counsel at that time.
The correctness of this record has not been rebutted or questioned by the defence at any stage of the trial.

Not even a single suggestion was given to any of the two PWs that the postal receipt Ex. PW-1/K was a forged or fabricated document or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.
It was only at the fag end of the case that the accused in his statement under section 313 CrPC claimed for the first time that he did not receive such a letter.
No PW was asked to produce the original record again if the accused had any doubt.
Thus, the accused cannot take benefit on this count.
17. Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
It is not the case of the accused that the said letter Ex. PW-1/J was sent at incorrect addresses.
No such stand has been taken by the accused at any stage of trial including prosecution evidence, statement of accused or defence evidence.
Rather the accused was served with court summons at the very address at which the intimation letter was sent.
Even the bail bond furnished by the accused discloses the same address.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at correct address through registered post.
But the accused has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by him to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letter was delivered or if it remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not delivered to the accused.
Accused has not Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj on 30 January, 2017

4 claimed that he was not staying at that address or was staying at some other address or that the letter could not have been served upon him at the relevant time.
It is not his claim that he was not available at the said address or had shifted from that address.
Thus, accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
As PW-1 and PW-2 deposed that the registered letter were sent, the burden would be upon the accused to prove anything to the contrary.
By not leading any evidence to support his stand, the version of the accused remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused in due course.
The accused cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by him.
18. This is not one of the cases where the accused was prevented from exercising his right under section 13(2) of PFA Act.
The accused has deliberately and voluntarily forgiven his right under section 13(2) of the Act.
Such argument is liable to be rejected.

19. In such an admitted set of factual matrix, it is also pertinent to note that the accused has not questioned the correctness of the PA report (though has disputed his opinion that the food article was adulterated) with respect to the presence of vegetable oil in the sample.
It is nowhere his case that no such vegetable oil was there in food article or that the vegetable oil had been wrongly detected or that some incorrect or unreliable method of analysis was used.
It is nowhere his defence that the besan laddus were containing some other ingredient like pista or almonds having vegetable oil whose oil entered into the food article.
It is again not his stand that such vegetable oil developed due to lapse of time.
He has not alleged that the samples were changed or that the said vegetable oil was added by the food officials at the time of sampling or by the laboratory staff at the time of testing.

A perusal of the cross-examination of the three PWs and the statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC would show that the accused has confined his defence only to one stand, that is,
the vegetable oil detected by the PA in the sample might have come from the tray on which vanaspati is usually applied by the workers to prevent laddus from sticking to the tray.

20. With such material in hand, it is clear that the food article "besan ke laddu" is not a standardised food article and thus, no standards have been prescribed under the PFA Rules which can be said to have been violated.
Since no standards have been prescribed for this commodity, it would be clear that section 2(ia)(m) of the PFA Act would not apply.
Such provision would be applicable only where the quality or purity of a food article falls below the prescribed standards.
But when there are no standards prescribed, there can be no violation under section 2(ia)(m).
But to say, that since there are no standards for this food article and thus there can be no adulteration, would certainly be not correct.
Even if a food article is not a standardised food article, it has to be free from adulteration and has to pass the other tests upon being considered as a proprietary food.

It cannot be said that since there are no standards prescribed for a particular food article, a seller is free to add poison/insects/putrid substance to it or sell it by injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.

The only benefit which the accused can get in case of such proprietary food is that there cannot ordinarily be a violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act which pertains to violation of prescribed standards.

sentences.text: Similarly, there is no evidence to show that the vegetable oil found in the food article was injuriously affecting the nature, substance or quality of the food article so as to bring it within purview of section 2(ia)(b), or that such vegetable oil was an inferior or cheaper substance which had been substituted for the food article so as to bring it under section 2(ia)(c) of PFA Act.
No such opinion has been given by the PA nor is there any evidence to this effect.

22. As far as Section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act is concerned, the prosecution has to establish that the besan ke laddu sold ("Sale" as per section 2(xiii) of PFA Act includes sale for analysis, offer for sale,
exposing for sale and attempt to sell) by the accused was not of the nature, substance or quality which it represented to be.

23. It is to be seen that when the Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW1/B was prepared and given to the accused vendor, upon asking of the FI PW-2, he himself and in his own handwriting disclosed the ingredients of the food article being sold by him.
He informed that the besan ke laddu had been prepared using Besan, Sugar and Ghee.
Apparently, he never disclosed presence of any vegetable oil in the food article.
As stated by PW-2, the ingredients were disclosed by the accused and this fact has never been denied by the accused.

It is not the case of the accused that such an ingredient had been disclosed by him or that he had forgotten to mention vegetable oil as an ingredient or that the FI did not write complete ingredients as disclosed by him or that he was forced or threatened or pressurized to write incomplete ingredients.
No such stand has been taken at any stage of trial nor any representation was made to the PFA Department between the date of lifting of the sample and filing of the complaint.
No such defence has been raised even at the trial in the court.

Therefore, if some vegetable oil is detected by the chemical expert which remains unexplained and which could not be attributed to the disclosed ingredients, then such presence of vegetable oil would be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of the Act.
24. There is no merit in the argument of Ld. Counsel that a vendor is not required to disclose the ingredients of sweets in view of Rule 43(5) of PFA Rules.

This Rule deals with declarations that are required to be given in case of packed food in advertisements, price list, trade list, etc. in case of food article which contains an addition, admixture or deficiency which affects its purity.
This rule pertains to declarations on the food package which is a prepackaged food within the definitions given under the Act and Rules.
But when a food article is sold in loose condition, as in the present case, no such Rule would apply as packaging and labelling standards are not applicable to such food being sold loose.
Rule 43 falls in Part-VII of PFA Rules that deals with packaging and labelling regulations.
Reliance on this Rule by the Ld. Counsel in this manner is misfounded.
There is nothing to show that a vendor selling sweets can escape from disclosing correct ingredients or to conceal some ingredients of a food product (unless it is a trade secret).
Thus, no benefit can be derived by the accused on this count.

25. Similarly, the court does not find force in the stand of the Ld. Defence Counsel that there is no standard for 'extract fat' and therefore, no sample can be failed due to presence of the such fat.

26. Well, it is correct that no standard has been prescribed for such extracted fat in food articles, but it is to be understood that the present case is not with respect to the any deficiency or adulteration Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj on 30 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65795867/
6 or sub- standardization in the extracted fact.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Rather the presence of fat in the form of vegetable oil in itself an issue here.
Irrespective of the quality of the extracted fat, the question here is how the fact was found in the food article when no such ingredient was disclosed by the vendor.
Here the court is not concerned if the extracted fat was of some other quality or nature.
The question is how the fat was found present when it was not declared as an ingredient.
This argument is without merit.
27. The only question to be determined now is, if the vegetable oil as detected by the PA could be that of the vanaspati which is claimed to be usually applied by the manufacturers to the tray.
28. It is to be understood that the PA is a chemical expert whose report is admissible in evidence without formal proof under section 293 CrPC.
However, it does not mean that the report can be taken as a gospel truth and cannot be questioned on any ground.
As per section 293 CrPC, the accused has an option to apply and cross examine the PA.
Thus, such a report can always be questioned to seek any clarification or to seek explanation on any point on which the report is silent or doubtful.
It is for the accused to avail this option available to him.
29. The PA is the best witness to explain the things, having examined the sample and having given opinion on the basis of analytical values.

PA would be the best person would accept or deny the stand taken by the accused, who would explain the intricacies and validity of the tests performed and who would justify the reasons for the opinion given.

30. As far as the contents of the PA report Ex. PW-1/G is concerned, it is to be understood that the report given by the PA is only the final report arrived after detailed analysis and is in the prescribed format as provided under the PFA Rules.
It is not that this report is the only material available with the PA on the analysis.

All the other details with respect to the tests conducted, the analytical values,
the calculations, etc. are recorded and maintained by the office of PA.
Such record can always be summoned from the office and can be proved and put to the PA during cross-examination.

31. Therefore, if the accused wishes to ascertain the details of the testing methods which do not form part of final report Ex. PW-1/G, he is required to exercise his option under section 293 CrPC to apply and cross- examine the PA and also to call for the records from the PA office either during the cross-examination of PA or even in his defence evidence.
But if the accused fails to exercise this option, he cannot now chose to dispute the PA report on the basis of any point on which the report is silent.
He cannot now question the report on any remote hypothesis, assumptions or presumptions.
32. The defence of the accused, that the workers had applied some vanaspati / vegetable oil on the tray to prevent laddus from sticking, in my considered view, has not been proved.
The BR value detected by PA in this case is 44.4.
After going through the entire material on record, the court fails to find any basis on which this BR value could be explained by the accused.
Various products have different BR values.
BR value of ghee (that was an ingredient of besan ke laddu, as disclosed by the accused on Ex. PW-1/B) in Delhi is 40-43.
Various oils like coconut oil, cottonseed oil, groundnut oil, linseed oil, olive oil, sunflower oil, etc have various BR values.
Most of these items are standardized food articles and the rules prescribe the range under which their BR values can fall.

However, there is nothing on record to show as to upto what extent the BR value of such a besan Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj on 30 January, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/65795867/
7 laddu would increase if some vanaspati in negligible quantities is applied to the surface of the tray

entities.text: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs Dev Raj
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
,
as claimed.
There is no evidence on record to show that the BR value of besan laddu or ghee would go high up to 44.4 from maximum 43.
If it was only a case of marginal increase, the court would still have assumed that the BR value increased due to some traces of vanaspati.
But the present is not of marginal increase.
33. The prosecution is required to prove its case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt and not to prove the case beyond all remotest probabilities and possibilities.

Of course there are several defences available to the accused, but the prosecution is not required to rule out all the said remote possibilities and defences under the Sun which the accused might claim at the trial.

If any specific defence has been taken by the accused, it would be for the accused to establish the same by either pointing out the defects / infirmities in the prosecution case and / or by leading defence evidence.
But the accused cannot claim that all the remote possibilities have to be ruled out by the prosecution.
34. During the evidence of PW-1 and PW-2, the accused never took any stand to the effect that the vegetable oil had been used by him as lubricant as GMP.
He never took stand that no vegetable oil was there in the food article as detected by the PA nor he questioned the PA report in any manner.
It was only during the evidence of PW-3 that the accused suggested to him that vanaspati was lying in the tray, which he categorically denied.
Thus, the accused has virtually accepted that there was vanaspati in the food article.
35. In any case, there is no evidence led by the accused to prove his defence.
He never gave any suggestion to any PW that the workers had applied vanasapti to the tray or if such a fact had been disclosed by him to the FI at the time of sampling or during investigation.
True, vegetable oil can be used under GMP but the question is, if the accused ever took such a stand at the trial.

Apparently,
not a single suggestion was put to any of the three PWs to the effect that the accused had used vegetable oil as a lubricant under GMP.
It was only when the evidence was over that the accused claimed in the statement for the first time by making positive statement that his workers had applied some vegetable oil on the tray.

But other than this explanation given under section 313 CrPC, which obviously cannot be termed as 'evidence', there is no positive material on the basis of which the court may conclude that vegetable oil had been used in the present case as a lubricant which had entered into the food article so as to increase the BR value as opined by the PA to such an extent.
No worker has been examined in defence who might have pasted vegetable oil on the tray as lubricant.
There is no witness who was present at the time of manufacturing of the commodity or who had seen any worker applying vegetable oil on the tray as a lubricant.
Therefore, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness who could establish that the vegetable oil found by the PA in the sample was on account of such use of oil as a lubricant.
No name of any such worker has been disclosed by the accused so as to enable the court to summon and examine him.

Therefore,
such a stand has to be rejected being without any evidentiary support and being only a bald averment.
Therefore, he sold a food article which was not of the quality, nature or substance which he represented to be.
This would, therefore, be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act.
36. No other stand has been taken by the accused at the trial or during the arguments advanced.

sentences.text: In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had stored / exposed for sale adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.

38. Thus, the accused is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a)
of the PFA Act.
39.
Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence.

But when there are no standards prescribed, there can be no violation under section 2(ia)(m).
Even if a food article is not a standardised food article, it has to be free from adulteration and has to pass the other tests upon being considered as a proprietary food.
It cannot be said that since there are no standards prescribed for a particular food article, a seller is free to add poison/insects/putrid substance to it or sell it by injuriously affecting its nature, substance or quality.
The only benefit which the accused can get in case of such proprietary food is that there cannot ordinarily be a violation of section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act which pertains to violation of prescribed standards.
Similarly, there is no evidence to show that the vegetable oil found in the food article was injuriously affecting the nature, substance or quality of the food article so as to bring it within purview of section 2(ia)(b), or that such vegetable oil was an inferior or cheaper substance which had been substituted for the food article so as to bring it under section 2(ia)(c) of PFA Act.
22. As far as Section 2(ia)(a) of the PFA Act is concerned, the prosecution has to establish that the besan ke laddu sold ("Sale" as per section 2(xiii) of PFA Act includes sale for analysis, offer for sale,
exposing for sale and attempt to sell) by the accused was not of the nature, substance or quality which it represented to be.
Therefore, if some vegetable oil is detected by the chemical expert which remains unexplained and which could not be attributed to the disclosed ingredients, then such presence of vegetable oil would be a violation of section 2(ia)(a) of the Act.
Rule 43 falls in Part-VII of PFA Rules that deals with packaging and labelling regulations.
There is nothing to show that a vendor selling sweets can escape from disclosing correct ingredients or to conceal some ingredients of a food product (unless it is a trade secret).
28. It is to be understood that the PA is a chemical expert whose report is admissible in evidence without formal proof under section 293 CrPC.
However, it does not mean that the report can be taken as a gospel truth and cannot be questioned on any ground.
Thus, such a report can always be questioned to seek any clarification or to seek explanation on any point on which the report is silent or doubtful.
It was only when the evidence was over that the accused claimed in the statement for the first time by making positive statement that his workers had applied some vegetable oil on the tray.
But other than this explanation given under section 313 CrPC, which obviously cannot be termed as 'evidence', there is no positive material on the basis of which the court may conclude that vegetable oil had been used in the present case as a lubricant which had entered into the food article so as to increase the BR value as opined by the PA to such an extent.
There is no witness who was present at the time of manufacturing of the commodity or who had seen any worker applying vegetable oil on the tray as a lubricant.
Therefore, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness who could establish that the vegetable oil found by the PA in the sample was on account of such use of oil as a lubricant.
No name of any such worker has been disclosed by the accused so as to enable the court to summon and examine him.
Therefore,
such a stand has to be rejected being without any evidentiary support and being only a bald averment.
Therefore, he sold a food article which was not of the quality, nature or substance which he represented to be.
It has been proved that the accused had stored / exposed for sale adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
